Hi All,

A while ago Russ Norvell asked about running the Distance analysis engine from
within other programming environments (below). I replied to him, but he didn't
summarize the replies he got to the list yet, so I thought I'd put my message on
the list as it may help others (see below). (Russ - could you please post any
other useful information you've gleaned?)

I've also written a very short Visual Basic project which gives an example of
one approach (that of making calls to the windows API). You can find it on the
Distance web site, under Distance Support | General. Hope someone finds it
useful!

- Len

==================BEGIN FORWARDED MESSAGE==================

> >Greetings all-

> >I'm hoping someone has successfully used another program (I'm thinking
> >of using R, possibly VBA?) to call the MCDS or earlier versions of the
> >Distance analysis engine in order to run 1000's of simulations,
> >bootstraps, etc. I've been through the List archive and seen a couple
> >suggestive posts, but nothing to imply that these have been brought to
> >fruition.

> >We'd like to look at the (admittedly retrospective) effects of
> >different study designs on estimates of annual bird density. To start,
> >we hope to look at the effect of number of survey visits within a
> >breeding season (up to 5 at a given study site) and number of point
> >transect sub-samples (up to 10 at a given study site) on our annual
> >density estimates. I suspect someone has already accomplished much of
> >this, but if not I'll ask around for a proper programmer.

> >Any thoughts? Thanks in advance

Hi Russell,

I'm replying just to you (not the list) to give you a few leads and provide you
with the info I can -- please can you collate all the information you get and
forward it to the list at some point, so others can benefit -- thanks!

Okay, first to others who I know of - only two I'm afraid:

- Paul Luckacs at Colorado State developed some simulation software, WebSim, to
look at the optimal spacing of traps in trapping web studies. In that he
simulates data and then calls the Distance analysis engine (D4.exe) to do the
analysis. The program is written in C++ I think. You can find out more, and
contact Paul, via his web page http://www.cnr.colostate.edu/~plukacs/web.html

- Tiago Marques here at St Andrews developed some quick and dirty code to do a
double platform analysis for someone in the Sea Mammal Research Unit here. The
code does a special type of bootstrap and for each bootstrap rep calls D4.exe to
do the analysis. It's written in VB. Tiago is a student here, and you can get
his email address from the Directory page of the school web site
http://www-maths.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/

Secondly, as to how you might go about it (assuming you want to/have to develop
code from scratch).

As you probably know, the CDS and MCDS analysis engine live in a separate
executable file D4.exe (written in FORTRAN), which is in the Distance program
directory. When you call D4.exe you pass in the location of a text file called
the command file which contains a bunch of lines of text telling distance what
analysis to do and also where a second file called the data file lives. The
data file (obviously enough) contains the data to use in that analysis, in "flat
file" format. All that happens when you press the "Run" button in Distance is
that Distance generates the appropriate files and then calls D4.exe. This is
documented in the online help on the page "Running the analysis engines as a
stand-alone program" (towards the end of Chapter 8).

Probably the best way to see what the command and data files should look like is
to get Distance to generate a template. In Distance, if you choose Tools |
Preferences and then the Analysis tab, and then tick the box "Debug mode", the
next time you run an analysis, Distance will generate the command and data
files, but will not run the analysis engine. In the Log tab of the Analysis
details, Distance will tell you where it's put the files (usually in your temp
directory) so you can have a look at them. The format of the command file is
pretty-much documented in the Distance 2.2 Users Guide, which you can download
from the Distance web site (under Distance 2.2). There have been a few changes:
- in batch mode (what we're using) the output files are not given in ASSIGN
statements but in the first few lines of the command file (as documented in the
online help page)
- the flat file format for the data file
- there are some new commands for MCDS analyses
The best way to get a handle on these last two is to generate some template
files as described above and see what's in them. One of these days I'll get
'round to writing an updated command manual... Meanwhile if you get problems
just drop me a line.

In many simulation applications, what you want to do is generate lots of
datasets, run the same analysis on each one, store the results, and then do some
summary statistics on the results. If you really want to run the same analysis
on each simulated dataset, then you just need to get Distance to generate the
right template command file and just use that -- otherwise your program will
have to write its own command file which can be trickier. In any case you will
have to write the data to a text file in the flat file format D4.exe expects --
you can put it where you like so long as you edit the INFILE command in the
command file. As for harvesting results, D4.exe puts out results into two
files: the results file and the stats file. The former is the long text file
that Distance displays in the Results page of the Analysis Details. The second
is a compact fixed-format summary (Distance harvests these results and uses them
to put out the summary statistics in the Analysis Browser -- but you don't need
to know that!). I suggest you use the latter as it is much easier to write a
program to parse this file. The format of the stats file is documented in the
online help on the page "Saving Results to File" (Chapter 8). You can also try
running an analysis from the command line, using the template files you've got
Distance to output, and then check out what it looks like for yourself.

Last thing is how to get your simulation program to run D4.exe. Most computer
languages have a "shell" command or some such, which allows them to run
programs. One problem with these is that often they start the external program
and then return control immediately to the calling routine. In your situation
you'd rather have something that waited for the analysis to finish before
returning. One solution (implemented by Tiago) is to simply have a "pause"
command and the next command after shell, causing the program to wait for a few
seconds before continuing -- in the hope that D4.exe will have finished by then.
This is simple, but a bit kludgy. A second alternative is to use Windows API
(application programming interface - a lowish-level interface to Windows) to do
it -- this takes some knowledge of how to program the Windows API. (Hint, if
you do go down this route: if you run D4.exe with CreateProcess (and then
WaitForInputIdle), you can wait for it to finish using WaitForSingleObject with
the timeout set to INFINITY.) A third way is to use the .dll which I've already
written to do the job (it's called D4CDSNEI.dll - NEI is short for numerical
engine interface). It is event driven, so you call a RunEngine method and then
wait for an event called RunFinished to fire. If you're writing in an event
driven language such as VB then that's probably the easiest way. I've put some
more information about this option at the bottom of this message, and can send
the source code if this would help.

Hope this helps to get you started -- if you have any more questions then give
me a shout. If you get desperate, I can probably do the programming (or at
least the bulk of it which you can then modify) as a short contract.

- Len

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Using D4CDSNEI.dll

It is an ActiveX dll, so any language that talks ActiveX will be able to use it.
For example, in a Visual Basic project, you choose Project | References, and
scroll down until you see "Distance 4 CDS Numerical Engine Interface" and tick
the box by that entry. Then, if you use the VB object browser, you will see
that D4CDSNEI contains a class called CDSProcess, with methods RunEngine and
KillEngine, a property ErrMsg and an event RunFinished. I've put the
documentation from my code below you can see more about the class. I can send
all the code if you think it would be useful -- the rest of that .dll contains
stuff for getting settings out of a model definition and data filter and combing
them to make a command file, for putting together a data file, for calling
CDSProcess, and for parsing the results, stats and plot file to store results.


'-------------------------------------------------------------------------
'CDS Numerical Engine Process class - CDSProcess
'-------------------------------------------------------------------------

'Purpose: Class that represent the analysis engine process. Contains
' API routines that start the analysis and wait for it to finish. Also
' routines to stop it if necessary.

'This class is declared as public because it is not only used internally
' by CDSNEngineInterface, but it is also used in the Distance interface/
' project database for importing old D22 data.

'Interface:
' Properties:
' ErrMsg As String (read-only)
' If Status Is FileError Then
' should contain an error message giving information about
' where the error occured - this could be saved into the Log file.
' Methods:
' RunEngine (EngineFile As String,
' Infile As String, Optional ByVal Import As Boolean = False,
' Optional ByVal CommandLineFile As String="")
' - Starts the engine run - set Import to true if you want to import
' an old distance file
' - EngineFile is the exe name -- without the path (assume the engine
' is located in App.Path)
' - CommandLineFile is a file to put command line output into if
' the engine is run under WinNT
' KillEngine - Stops a run and kills the engine process
' Events:
' RunFinished (EngineStatus As CDSEngineStatus)
' - Raised when a run has finished.
